title: Ohio v. EPA (2024)
summary: An agency rule is likely arbitrary and capricious when the agency fails to give a reasoned response to a significant comment about a premise of its plan, so the Court stayed enforcement of EPA's Good Neighbor Plan against the challengers pending review.
notes:
Key line: "But awareness is not itself an explanation." (Gorsuch, J.)

Citation: 603 U.S. 279 (2024).

sections.Parties: The applicants were Ohio, Indiana and West Virginia, joined by industry applicants including Kinder Morgan, Inc., the American Forest and Paper Association, and United States Steel Corporation, in four consolidated applications, Nos. 23A349, 23A350, 23A351 and 23A384. The respondents were the Environmental Protection Agency and its Administrator, supported by New York and other downwind states, New York City, and public interest respondents including the Environmental Defense Fund. The applications sought a stay of EPA's federal implementation plan pending review in the D.C. Circuit. The Energy Infrastructure Council filed an amicus brief supporting a stay.
sections.Material Facts: The Clean Air Act's Good Neighbor Provision requires each State Implementation Plan to prohibit emissions that contribute significantly to nonattainment in other states. After EPA revised the ozone standard in 2015, states submitted new plans. In February 2022 EPA proposed to disapprove 21 plans, and two more states had filed none. In April 2022, during the comment period on those disapprovals, EPA proposed a single Federal Implementation Plan for all 23 states, choosing emissions controls by identifying the cost level at which further reductions across the group produced diminishing returns in downwind ozone. Commenters warned that if some states dropped out the analysis would have to be redone. EPA issued the final plan on June 5, 2023, adding only a severability clause stating that the plan would continue to apply to remaining states. By the time of decision courts had stayed disapprovals for 12 of the 23 states, accounting for more than 70 percent of the targeted emissions.
sections.Procedural History: The remaining states and industry groups petitioned the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit for review of the federal plan under 42 U.S.C. section 7607, arguing that applying it after so many states had dropped out was arbitrary or capricious, and moved for a stay pending review. The D.C. Circuit denied a stay. The applicants renewed their requests in the Supreme Court, which received more than 400 pages of briefing, heard oral argument on the applications on February 21, 2024, and on June 27, 2024, granted the stays by a vote of 5 to 4, staying enforcement of the rule against the applicants pending disposition of the petitions in the D.C. Circuit and any timely petition for certiorari.
sections.Issue: Whether the applicants were entitled to a stay under the Nken v. Holder factors, which in this case turned on whether they were likely to succeed on their claim that EPA's final Federal Implementation Plan was arbitrary or capricious because EPA never explained whether the emissions controls it chose, calibrated to maximize cost effective ozone improvement across 23 states, remained appropriate when the plan applied to only about half of them; and whether EPA's severability clause, the Act's reasonable specificity requirement for comments, or the requirement to seek agency reconsideration for objections arising after the comment period defeated that claim.
sections.Holding: The Court granted the stays. Because the harms and equities were weighty on both sides, the decision turned on the merits, and the applicants were likely to prevail. Under FCC v. Prometheus Radio Project and State Farm, agency action must be reasonable and reasonably explained and may not ignore an important aspect of the problem. Commenters raised the concern that the knee in the curve might shift if states dropped out, and EPA offered no reasoned response; at argument the government could not say whether its analysis would yield the same results for a single state. The severability clause showed awareness but supplied no explanation, the objection was raised with reasonable specificity, and the applicants did not have to return to EPA to raise again a concern it had already had a chance to address.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Gorsuch explained that EPA's plan rested on the assumption that all 23 upwind states would adopt controls up to a uniform cost level at the point of diminishing returns, and each state differs in its industries, existing controls and downwind impact, so a different set of states might move the knee in the curve. Awareness of a problem is not itself an explanation, and nothing in the severability discussion addressed whether measures found cost effective with 23 participants remained so with far fewer. EPA could not rely on explanations published in 2024 after argument because the Act confines the record to material docketed at promulgation. On the reasonable specificity requirement, the Court cited Appalachian Power Co. v. EPA for the rule that a party need not rehearse the identical argument, only give the agency notice in substance; comments urging a new assessment and modeling if states fell out, together with EPA's own statement that it had considered applying the plan to a subset of states, showed such notice. The reconsideration requirement applies to objections arising after the comment period, not to objections the agency already had a chance to address. The Court declined to consider the dissent's theories that the methodology did not depend on the number of states or that any error was harmless, because the government had not made those arguments despite voluminous briefing, and because the government's own uncertainty at argument counseled caution.

topics.lrs-n-hard-look: At the stay stage, the majority found likely failure to answer an important comment, while the dissent disputed the premise and record.
topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-record: The stay turned on EPA's failure to respond to significant comments about whether the plan would still be justified if fewer states were covered.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 5 to 4. Justice Barrett dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson. She argued that the Court granted emergency relief on an underdeveloped theory unlikely to succeed: the commenters had criticized the sequencing of the disapprovals and the plan rather than the number of covered states, so the objection was not preserved and should have gone to EPA on a motion for reconsideration; EPA's cost effectiveness methodology used nationwide data and did not appear to depend on which states were included, so any failure to explain was neither important nor prejudicial; and the Court's own cited comments concerned variances among facilities and industries rather than states. She also emphasized EPA's statutory duty to issue a federal plan when state plans fail and noted that no court had yet invalidated a disapproval.
